stage_state.summary_md:
## Coordination and Announcement

BA sought to coordinate retirement with Air France, aiming for October (end of summer schedule). Air France agreed, then chose May instead—reflecting divergent attitudes; in France, a dual retirement perceived as celebratory was never sanctioned post-accident.

BA planned to announce at a Forum 150 meeting (top 150 managers) on 9th April 2003. Bannister pointed out this was the 34th anniversary of the British Concorde's first flight, so it moved to 10th April. Bannister, in uniform, presented the rationale via slides. Senior management split roughly two-thirds sad, one-third relieved—no ambivalence, presaging public reaction.

## Public Messaging and Key Questions

Bannister became company spokesman. Key messages: the decision was commercial, spurred by factors beyond BA's control; customers would be served via upgraded 747 Club Class and First. At the press conference, asked why she was being retired, Bannister said: 'It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons'—the party line, despite his earlier internal view that it was the wrong decision for wrong reasons.

Common questions: 'Why spend money returning Concorde to service only to retire it less than two years later?' and 'If numbers don't add up, why not retire immediately?' BA's answer: retirement was for sound commercial reasons, not due to the accident.

## Branson and Single-Aircraft Retention

On Branson's offer: BA's party line was that the UK government funded the aircraft, so transfer wasn't BA's decision. Bannister privately told a Virgin pilot 'not a chance in hell'; the pilot replied 'Thank God, because it would probably send us bust!'—which Bannister believed likely.

On retaining one aircraft: Concorde required a Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate, far costlier than the Permit to Fly used by the Avro Vulcan. Infrastructure cost was £60 million per annum, about to rise by another £40 million—the same for one aircraft as for seven. Airbus, the Type Certificate holder, was uninterested; its focus was on the A380 and A320 family. Concorde's air-intake computer technology was proprietary and secret, used on military aircraft Airbus produced. There was no upside for Airbus—'nobody would ever say at an air show, “Look, there goes an Airbus Concorde!”'

## Legacy and Public Sentiment

As summer approached, public discussion shifted to Concorde's legacy. People talked about 'the wonderful job UK plc had done'; conversations began with 'I never got to fly on Concorde myself, sadly, but I know someone whose Aunt Mabel once flew on it…' BA ensured a celebration of all associated people—designers, builders, operators, engineers, cabin crew, baggage handlers, ticket agents, and the public.

Edward de Bono told Bannister Concorde appealed to both brain hemispheres—technologically superb and artistically graceful. Bannister's simpler view: most Brits felt a sense of ownership—'That's my Concorde up there.'
